#### 4.13.2 Which finish is "the finish": basic or production dates, float, lead time, and SAP's own reversal

**The question.** SAP planning can carry more than one date pair for an order, and the gap between them is scheduling margin (float). SAP's lead time is normally built from master data and can include setup, queue and move time **[unverified: needs SAP Development]**. The Functional Specification names one start and one finish ("Order start date in the planned order", "Order finish date in the planned order") and never says which pair. NIMBUS treats the finish it receives as the due date (O4), the start as SAP's information, and sends back a finish only. The whole echo premise (SAP stores the finish it was sent and returns it) rests on this.

**Which date pair crosses in each direction, per the Functional Specification.**

| Direction | The Functional Specification says | What NIMBUS reads or writes | What is not stated |
|---|---|---|---|
| SAP to NIMBUS (export, FSD 6.5) | Order start date and start time; order finish date and end time | Start into the stored SAP start and its baseline; finish into the stored due date and its baseline; both converted from the SAP zone | Whether these are the basic dates or the production (scheduled) dates; whether the end time is populated |
| NIMBUS to SAP (import, FSD 7.2, 7.3) | End date, end time, production version, firm indicator; the order is found by product, location and order number | The stored placed finish today the computed end (4.5.4), the version, the firm rule | Start and quantity are not sent, so SAP must derive its own start. Whether the import writes the basic or the production finish, and whether SAP then adds or removes float, is not stated (validation assumption A9 assumes only that SAP "back-schedules the start") |

**Four systematic differences between SAP's pair and NIMBUS's pair. All are assumptions the document had been treating as settled.**

1. **Float.** If the finish NIMBUS sends is read as a basic finish and SAP applies float to derive its production finish (or the reverse), the finish SAP exports next time differs from the one it was sent. That is rule 2 of 4.13.1 (a genuine SAP change): the placement is wiped and the due date is replaced by SAP's returned value.
2. **Lead time against run time.** SAP's lead time can include setup and queue time. NIMBUS's run time is production hours at the one work center the machine maps to, with setup never counted (`ROUTING_RUNTIME_DESIGN.md:21`, `:229-231`; `aggregate_to_detail.md:657`). For the same finish SAP's start would be earlier than NIMBUS's derived start by the setup and queue time. That difference is systematic, so SAP's start can never be used as a check on the derived start.
3. **SAP's own reversal.** If SAP's lead time, counted back from the finish NIMBUS sent, puts SAP's start before today, SAP may schedule forward from today and return a later finish. That returned finish differs from the sent one, so NIMBUS reads a genuine SAP change and wipes the placement, and "the finish NIMBUS sent never moves" is overridden on SAP's side with nothing NIMBUS can do about it. The only repository source for SAP's "backward-with-reversal" is a note about the APO planning system (`docs/SAP_APO_Opportunities.md:48`); the pilot interface is ECC (the Functional Specification's title). Whether ECC planned-order rescheduling flips forward, from which "today", with what rounding or tolerance, is not documented **[unverified: needs SAP Development]**. O2 named the behaviour "SAP's backward-with-reversal" without saying which SAP engine is copied (Appendix D, D.1 item 6).
4. **Rounding and tolerance.** If SAP rounds a finish to a minute, an hour or a factory-calendar boundary (assumption A9), the minute-exact echo test never matches; its tolerance today is under one minute (a 40-second difference is tolerated, one minute is not: `tests/test_orders_routing_ingest.py:599-640`).

**Worked example (all SAP figures are invented to show the mechanism; none is an SAP result).** Planner places Order Z to finish Thu 22 Oct 12:00 and presses Send on Tue 20 Oct. *Case 1, SAP stores the finish as sent:* it sets its own start and exports Thu 22 Oct 12:00 next time; echo, placement kept. *Case 2, SAP's lead time for the order is 3 working days (setup, queue and run) and SAP reverses:* counted back from Thu 12:00 the start would be Fri 16 Oct, which is in the past, so SAP schedules forward from Tue 20 Oct and exports a finish of Fri 23 Oct 12:00. NIMBUS reads a genuine SAP change, wipes the placement, stores Fri 23 Oct 12:00 as the new due date (as received) and shows the order unplaced. The planner's Thursday 12:00 is gone and no setting inside NIMBUS prevented it.

**What the document had stated as fact.** 2.2 ("The SAP round trip"), 4.5.1(c) and 4.5.10 describe SAP back-scheduling its start to Wed 16:00 and echoing Thu 12:00. The Wed 16:00 figure is NIMBUS's own arithmetic (20 elapsed hours before the finish); 4.5.1 and 2.2 now label it illustrative. The echo itself was measured only against a simulator that echoed every finish "exactly as sent" (`docs/SAP_STAGING_VALIDATION_PLAN.md:148`). The consequence line the document already carries ("if SAP moves the finish, every Send resets every sent order", 4.5.3 and Appendix D) is why 4.13.8 promotes assumption A9 to a gate before Send goes live.

**Multi-operation routings.** NIMBUS draws one bar per order and one finish per order. Its run time is the sum of the operations at the one work center the order's machine maps to; operations at other work centers are ignored (`ROUTING_RUNTIME_DESIGN.md:21`, `:229-231`). Whether SAP's planned-order finish is the end of the last operation anywhere in the routing, or of the work center NIMBUS plans, is not documented **[unverified: needs SAP Development]**. What NIMBUS sends is the finish of the bar it draws, which is the finish of the work NIMBUS knows about. An order whose routing continues at another work center after NIMBUS's operation could therefore be sent an earlier order finish than SAP's last operation allows. This is a stated limit of the model (single work center), not a defect to fix in this migration.

Evidence:
- `fsd2.txt:195-204` (FSD 6.5): `"Order start date in the planned order / PLAF-PSTTR"` and `"Order finish date in the planned order / PLAF-PEDTR"`; `fsd2.txt:270-279`: `"Start Time / PLAF-PSTTI"`, `"End Time / PLAF-PEDTI"`. `fsd2.txt:343-366` (FSD 7.2): the import's update values are Production Version, End Date, End Time, Firm Indicator; `:373-377` (7.3) lists the same four updates.
- `docs/SAP_STAGING_DESIGN.md:161`: `"psttr + pstti → basic_start_date (composite, zone-converted), pedtr + pedti → basic_finish_date and the SAP finish baseline"`; `:163`: `"effective end (zone-converted) → pedtr + pedti"`.
- `ROUTING_RUNTIME_DESIGN.md:231`: "There is no fallback between the two, no other category counts, and setup time is never used at any step."; `:229`: `run_time  = Σ_ops hours(op), rounded to the nearest minute`; `:21` (D1): "Operations at the SAP work center that the order's NIMBUS machine maps to".
- `docs/SAP_APO_Opportunities.md:48`: "APO placement searches run forward, backward, or **backward-with-reversal** (search backward from the due date; if the search hits "now," flip to forward)."
- `docs/SAP_STAGING_VALIDATION_PLAN.md:42`: "A9 | The SAP import updates only End Date/Time, Version and Firm, and SAP then back-schedules the start (D20 rationale) | If SAP also moves the finish to a factory-calendar boundary, the echo never matches and every Send causes a reset wave | Send one order, read the next export, diff all fields | SAP Dev"; `:148`: "SAP echoed every finish exactly as sent".
- `db.py:2649-2653`: `def _minute(v): ... return v.replace(second=0, microsecond=0)` then `_minute(in_f) == _minute(sent_f)`.

#### 4.13.3 Infinite against finite capacity, and a derived start earlier than SAP's start

**The difference.** NIMBUS places orders on finite machines and sequences them; SAP schedules each planned order against its own lead time and does not level capacity unless a levelling run is made **[unverified: needs SAP Development: whether any capacity levelling runs on the pilot plants' planned orders]**. The repository's design record accepts the consequence in one direction only: NIMBUS "copies SAP's dates as a ceiling and never rescales them; a parent SAP planned serially will look early in NIMBUS, which is acceptable" (`aggregate_to_detail.md:482`, `:659`). That sentence is about the finish of distributed orders. Nothing equivalent is written for a start.

**Why the backward rule makes the start question new.** Today an order starts where SAP starts it (the stored SAP start is the default bar start) unless the planner moves it. Under the new rule the start is derived backward from the finish, so it lands before SAP's start whenever the run time (plus closed hours and setup) is longer than SAP's window. For the pilot sample this is the usual case: for 585 of 593 COOIS rows the SAP window is shorter than the Machine Hours (8.11; the workbook may be a different order type from the pilot feed, 4.13.7). A derived start earlier than SAP's start can mean the material is not yet available: SAP's own start can reflect component availability, and the export carries an availability-check flag that NIMBUS stores and never reads **[unverified: needs SAP Development: what the flag and SAP's start encode]**. No opening date or earliest-start field is in the Functional Specification's export list, so NIMBUS has nothing from SAP with which to say "do not start before".

| Question | Today | Under the new rule | Anchors |
|---|---|---|---|
| Can a bar start before SAP's start? | Only if the planner drags it there; the default bar starts at SAP's start | Yes, by construction, whenever run time exceeds SAP's window | 4.13.2; 8.11; `aggregate_to_detail.md:659` |
| Is it flagged? | The optimizer's pull floor limits how far left it moves an order, per plant (`max_pull_forward_days`); a manual drag is not checked | No alert type covers it (4.10.1 lists none) | 4.8.4; 4.10.1 |
| Which start does the planner see after an echo? | The bar shows the stored start; SAP's own start is overwritten by every written snapshot (`db.py:2828`) and appears nowhere on screen | The bar shows the derived start; SAP's start is again hidden | `orders.mts:534-543`; 4.6.4 |

**Which start the planner sees after an echo.** After a Send and an echo, SAP's back-scheduled start replaces the stored SAP start and its baseline (`db.py:2828`, `2835`). The two "Original Start" surfaces do not show it: the grid column and the Inspector row show the due date minus the run time (`impliedOriginalStart`, `frontend/scheduling/orders.mts:543`; 4.6.4). The planner therefore has no on-screen way to see "SAP starts this order at X". OQ16 recommends retiring Original Start altogether; if the owner wants a read-only "SAP starts at" line (for example to check material availability), it has to be added deliberately, and none is proposed here.

Evidence:
- `aggregate_to_detail.md:482`: "NIMBUS copies SAP's dates as a ceiling and never rescales them; a parent SAP planned serially will look early in NIMBUS, which is acceptable." `:659`: "NIMBUS copies SAP dates as a ceiling (§5.3, §13.22)."
- `db.py:2828`: `basic_start_date      = EXCLUDED.basic_start_date,`; `db.py:2835`: `sap_basic_start_date  = COALESCE(EXCLUDED.sap_basic_start_date, orders.sap_basic_start_date),`.
- `frontend/scheduling/orders.mts:543`: `valueGetter: (p: { data: NimbusTask }) => Util.impliedOriginalStart(p.data),`; `foundation.mts:632-638`: `return new Date(due.getTime() - Util.runHours(t) * Config.MS_HOUR);`.
- `fsd2.txt:295-299` (FSD 6.5): `"Availability Check / PLAF-KZAVC"`; a search of the repository's Python, TypeScript and SQL (outside `.venv`) for all eleven staging-only names finds each only in `schema.sql` and `migrations/2026-10-08-sap-staging-tables.sql`, so no code reads any staging-only column.

#### 4.13.4 The time-zone chain, end to end

Four sections of this document touch time zones one link at a time (4.2.5, 4.5.5, 4.5.9, 4.11). This is the whole chain in one table. Rows are in the order a finish travels from SAP to a planner's screen and back. A row marked **[unverified]** is an assumption nothing in the repository settles.

| # | Link | The assumption | Code anchor | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | SAP system zone | Dates and times in the planned-order records are in one fixed SAP system zone, not the plant's. The code default is UTC "until SAP Development confirms" | `sap_staging.py:78` (`NIMBUS_SAP_SYSTEM_TZ`, default `UTC`); design D34; validation A4 | **[unverified: needs SAP Basis]**. The Functional Specification never mentions a zone |
| 2 | SAP to Mulesoft (export) and Mulesoft to SAP (import) | Mulesoft passes the date and time through unchanged in both directions (no conversion to UTC, no offset suffix) | `docs/NIMBUS_INTERFACE_ARCHITECTURE.md:520` states the contract NIMBUS expects; nothing records what Mulesoft does | **[unverified: needs the integration owner]** |
| 3 | Staging tables | The zone is by convention only: the date and time columns are raw text with no zone attribute; a time of `000000` or blank means "date only" | `migrations/2026-10-08-sap-staging-tables.sql` (`pedtr`, `pedti` are `TEXT`); `sap_staging.py:184-207` | Code fact; the convention is unverified |
| 3b | The horizon edge | SAP's "today" for its planning horizon and NIMBUS's anchor day for the visibility horizon agree to within the one day of slack. NIMBUS's edge is a plant-zone date rolled once a day at a UTC hour | `db.py:422-457` (`_horizon_boundary_core`); design D8, D22; validation A5, A11 | **[unverified: the SAP side]** |
| 4 | Staging to plant | A time present is converted SAP zone to plant zone. A date-only value is not converted. A plant with no zone gets no conversion at all, with no warning | `sap_staging.py:210-227`; `backend/integration/CLAUDE.md` limit L10; `schema.sql:274` (`plants.timezone` is nullable) | Code fact. Count of plants with no zone: unknown (profile P2 below) |
| 5 | Stored values | Orders' stored dates are naive plant-local wall-clock values | `db.py:3198-3199`; `db.py:2580-2596` (`_naive_dt`) | Code fact |
| 6 | Plant to browser | The browser reads those naive strings as its own local time. Calendar math uses the viewer's local getters, so the walk follows the viewer's clock, not the plant's (4.2.5) | `frontend/optimization/engine.mts:1018`, `1288-1311`; `foundation.mts:745-764` | Code fact; a viewer in another zone sees running and frozen flip by the offset |
| 7 | Browser to server | The browser writes naive local strings; rows saved before 2026-07-07 by a non-UTC client are shifted by that client's offset, with no per-row offset to invert | `frontend/platform/foundation.mts:375-380` (`toLocalSeconds`); `docs/MIGRATION.md:984-989` | Code fact; the historic exposure is unprofiled (R3-14) |
| 8 | Plant to SAP (Send) | The finish is converted plant to SAP zone to the second. The remembered sent finish is stored plant-local. A plant with no zone sends its plant-local clock as if it were SAP's | `sap_staging.py:230-242`, `2249`, `2256` | Code fact |
| 9 | Server "now" | Plant-local now; with no plant zone it falls back to UTC | `db.py:3198-3206` (`_plant_local_now`) | Code fact |
| 10 | Browser "now" | Reversal (O2), running and frozen need one "now". The code has several: the viewer's instant compared with naive plant wall-clock dates; a plant-projected clock in Remove Backlog (which throws if the plant has no zone); the optimizer's floored clock; a viewer-local fallback in the plant clock helper that returns hour and minute only | `engine.mts:1018`, `1293-1311`; `foundation.mts:745-764` | Decision pending: OQ52 |

**Plants with no time zone.** `plants.timezone` is nullable. A plant with none gets no SAP conversion in either direction (the same wall-clock digits are read and written), the server's "now" falls back to UTC (row 9), Remove Backlog refuses to run, and the plant clock shows the viewer's own time. O3 puts every plant in at once, so every such plant enters the new rule with a "now" that is not the plant's. The count is not known. Profile P2, read-only:

```sql
-- P2: plants with no usable zone (no SAP conversion; UTC fallback for "now")
SELECT plant, timezone FROM plants WHERE timezone IS NULL OR btrim(timezone) = '' ORDER BY plant;
-- and zones Postgres does not recognise (the browser and server may disagree about them)
SELECT p.plant, p.timezone FROM plants p
 WHERE p.timezone IS NOT NULL AND btrim(p.timezone) <> ''
   AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_timezone_names n WHERE n.name = p.timezone)
 ORDER BY p.plant;
```

**What goes wrong if one link is wrong.** If the SAP zone is not what the code assumes (row 1), every converted finish is off by the offset, the echo never matches, and the first apply resets everything (validation plan A4). If SAP discards the time of day (4.5.5, case 3), rows 1 to 4 turn a time-zone difference into a date difference. If a plant has no zone (row 4), SAP's clock and the plant's clock are treated as equal, which is consistent but wrong by the real offset, and a finish placed late in the plant's evening can land on the next calendar day in SAP.

**The zone of "now".** Row 10 is the part the document had not stated. Which clock decides "has this order's derived start passed" is an owner decision (OQ52); the evidence for it is rows 6, 9 and 10.

Evidence:
- `sap_staging.py:78`: `SAP_SYSTEM_TZ = os.getenv("NIMBUS_SAP_SYSTEM_TZ", "UTC")`; `sap_staging.py:222-227`: `if t is None: return naive` ... `if src is None or dst is None: return naive` ... `return naive.replace(tzinfo=src).astimezone(dst).replace(tzinfo=None)`; `sap_staging.py:241-242`: `out = out.replace(tzinfo=None, microsecond=0); return out.date(), out.time()`.
- `schema.sql:274`: `timezone           TEXT,` (no NOT NULL); `backend/integration/CLAUDE.md` L10: "a plant with no `timezone` gets no SAP-zone conversion in either direction (both sides stay consistent, no warning)".
- `db.py:3198-3206`: `"""Naive plant-local wall-clock now ... an unknown/missing timezone falls back to UTC like the horizon math."""`.
- `db.py:452`: `if now_utc.astimezone(timezone.utc).hour >= int(horizon_roll_hour_utc):`.

#### 4.13.5 Where an order's run time comes from, and what that does to a derived start

Under the backward rule the run time decides how far left the start goes, so an order's run-time provenance now matters. There are five sources. Only some are flagged.

| Source | When it applies | What it contains | How it is flagged | What a quantity change does to the derived start | Anchors |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Routing resolver | Plants with routing switched on | Sum of the hours of the operations at the machine's work center (machine or labor category), scaled by order quantity over base quantity; setup never counted | `orders.run_time_source = 'routing'` and a `run_time_basis` record shown read-only in the Inspector | The hours are re-scaled by the open quantity (total minus reduced). The new run time lands when the order is next resolved (an upload that changed it, or a plant recompute), and the held-finish rule then moves the start. A partial conversion changes the open quantity without resetting the order (design D15), so the start moves with no wipe and no notice | `backend/routing/resolver.py:123-158`, `300-302`; `schema.sql:1985-1990`; design D15 |
| Machine Hours on the routing fallback | Routing plants when the resolver cannot resolve (production version found, but steps 2 to 8 fail) | The file's Machine Hours value, read as machine time | `run_time_source = 'sap_order'` | None: the value comes from the file and is not scaled | `resolver.py:214-221` |
| Machine Hours on a routing-off plant | Manual Excel upload to a plant whose routing switch is off | Machine Hours when above 0, else the run-time column, else 1 hour (owner decision 2026-10-13); the unit is unconfirmed | One batch-level "info" line with a row count; no per-order marker was found | None until the next upload; a re-upload that changes it widens or narrows the bar in place (blocker 8) | `db.py:4141-4156`; `docs/SAP_STAGING_DESIGN.md` D23 |
| A retained manual value | Routing plants when the resolver cannot resolve and the order already holds a value the planner keyed | The planner's own value | `run_time_source = 'legacy'`; only a planner-keyed value is retained, any other stored value is held as "run time unknown" | None: it is kept as it is, even if the quantity has moved on | `resolver.py:222-233` |
| The 1.0 hour default | Excel upload only, when both the run-time column and Machine Hours are blank | 1.0 hour | Only the distribution path records it (`runtime_defaulted`); a plain order has no marker | None | `db.py:3975-3980`, `4047`; `backend/distribution/data.py:686-687`, `887` |

Notes. (1) The design document's fallback text (`ROUTING_RUNTIME_DESIGN.md:218`) says the fallback keeps "the order's existing run time"; the code keeps only a planner-keyed one and holds everything else (`resolver.py:222-233`). The code wins. (2) A planner-keyed value is dropped back to the resolver the next time SAP changes the order (`db.py:2864-2869`). (3) SAP staging rows never carry a run time, so the 1.0 hour default cannot reach an order that came through the planned-order feed; such a plant must have routing on or the batch is held (`sap_staging.py:728-734`, design D23).

**Why a defaulted run time is the dangerous one.** Under the backward rule a 1.0 hour default puts the start exactly one hour before the finish, which looks plausible and is wrong for any order that really runs for days. Nothing marks such an order on a plain Excel path, so the first sign is a short bar. The default is also what hygiene uses when it fabricates a finish (4.5.6), so the same wrong hour feeds the due date.

**How many orders sit in each class is not known.** Profile P3, read-only:

```sql
-- P3: run-time provenance per plant
SELECT plant, COALESCE(run_time_source, '(none)') AS source, count(*) AS orders,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE run_time IS NULL) AS no_run_time
  FROM orders GROUP BY plant, 2 ORDER BY plant, 2;
```

Evidence:
- `resolver.py:222-233`: `if existing_run_time and order.get("run_time_source") == "manual": return {"status": "fallback_legacy", ... "run_time_source": "legacy" ...}` ... `return {"status": "held", "reason_code": "runtime_unknown", "detail_step": reason_code}`; `resolver.py:214-221`: `machine_hours = order.get("machine_hours")` ... `"run_time_source": "sap_order"`.
- `resolver.py:156-158`: `return hours * qty / base_q, None` (the operation hours are multiplied by order quantity over base quantity); `resolver.py:300-302` passes `order.get("order_quantity")` to that function.
- `db.py:4141-4156`: `"Manual Excel upload only: Machine Hours (MEINH) wins over RUN_TIME when present and > 0"` and the `info` warning `"run time taken from Machine Hours (MEINH)"`.
- `db.py:3975-3980`: `df["_RUN_TIME_DEFAULTED"] = _rt.isna()` then `df["RUN_TIME"] = _rt.fillna(1.0)`; `distribution/data.py:686-687`: `if runtime_defaulted: sap_facts["runtime_defaulted"] = True`.
- `db.py:2864-2869`: the `run_time_source` arm: `WHEN orders.run_time_source = 'manual' AND {_ROUTING_PLANT_SQL} AND {_SAP_DIFFERS_SQL} THEN NULL`.
- `docs/SAP_STAGING_DESIGN.md` D15: "Scheduled quantity = **total minus reduced** ... a partial conversion ... does not unschedule the order".

#### 4.13.6 The Functional Specification against what this document describes

The Functional Specification (copy re-saved 2026-10-13, version 3.0) lists 25 fields in the planned-order export (6.5) and 4 update fields in the import (7.2). NIMBUS maps 14 of the 25 into live columns; 11 land in staging and nothing reads them (`docs/SAP_STAGING_DESIGN.md:161`; confirmed by a search of the Python, TypeScript and SQL for the staging-only names). Field codes appear only in the code column.

| FSD item | Code | Direction | What NIMBUS does today | Covered in this document |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Order start date, start time | `PLAF-PSTTR`, `PLAF-PSTTI` | Export | Combined into the stored SAP start and its baseline; zone-converted; blank or `000000` time means date only | 3.2, 4.5.5 |
| Order finish date, end time | `PLAF-PEDTR`, `PLAF-PEDTI` | Export and import | Export: stored due date and its baseline. Import: the finish NIMBUS sends | 3.2, 4.5.1 to 4.5.5 |
| Total planned order quantity | `PLAF-GSMNG` | Export | Stored as the total; a changed total resets the order | 4.5.1 (e), design D15 |
| Reduced quantity | `PLAF-ABMNG` | Export | Stored; open quantity is total minus reduced | 4.13.5 |
| Firming indicator | `PLAF-AUFFX` | Export and import | Export: stored, display only. Import: sent as X when the planner firmed, SAP already had it, or the start is inside the frozen window (add-only) | 4.11 |
| Production version | `PLAF-VERID` | Export and import | Stored with its baseline; the import sends the version | 4.5.12 |
| Order number, material, plant, production line | `PLAF-PLNUM`, `PLAF-MATNR`, `PLAF-PLWRK`, `MKAL-MDV01` | Export; import keys are product, location, order number | Order id is a hash of order number and material; line is the work-center value distribution resolves | 4.13.1, 4.7 |
| Bill of material usage, alternative | `PLAF-STLAN`, `PLAF-STALT` | Export | Stored as integers | none needed |
| **Fields the document ignores** | | | | |

| Committed quantity | `PLAF-VFMNG` | Export | Staging only | none |
| Procurement proposal type | `PLAF-PAART` | Export | Staging only. It may be what tells planned from production orders, which `aggregate_to_detail.md:664` records as not known **[unverified]** | 4.13.7 |
| Conversion indicator | `PLAF-UMSKZ` | Export | Staging only; relevant to a planned order converted to a production order (design D21) | 4.13.1 |

| Account assignment category | `PLAF-KNTTP` | Export | Staging only | none |
| Availability check | `PLAF-KZAVC` | Export | Staging only; may bear on a start earlier than SAP's (4.13.3) | 4.13.3 |
| Change via BAdI | `PLAF-BADI` | Export | Staging only; could mark an order whose dates an SAP enhancement changed, which is a "genuine SAP change" the echo test cannot tell from other changes **[unverified]** | none |
| APO creation date | `PLAF-DAC_Creation_Date` | Export | Staging only; could tell a freshly created order from an old one, which is the one signal that might help recognise a renumbered order (4.13.1) **[unverified: whether SAP populates it]** | none |
| **Plant table and horizons** | | | | |
| Planning horizon (days) | plant table, 3.3 | Gates the export (6.4) | NIMBUS uses its own `visibility_horizon_days`, "kept equal by hand" (design D22, validation A5); no code compares them | 4.5.8 |
| Frozen horizon (days) | plant table, 3.3 | None stated | NIMBUS's `frozen_horizon_days` is independent. The staging design never mentions an SAP-side frozen horizon, and nothing reads it. Whether SAP's planning run treats it as a time fence is unknown **[unverified: needs SAP Development]** | 4.11 |
| Export limit | 6.4 | Export | "Planning Horizon plus 1 day ... relative to the `PLAF-PEDTR` end-date": **cut off mid-sentence; see below** | 4.5.8 |
| Run cadence | 4.4, 5.4, 6.6, 7.6 | Both | "Scheduled via a Process Chain"; no frequency anywhere. Export RFC: "Presently unsure if Async or Sync". Import RFC: synchronous preferred, "timing/success of the ingestion is of high importance" | Appendix D, D.1 item 4 |
| Import error handling | 7.4, 7.5 | Import | An order not found is skipped and logged; a log file records each execution. No per-row result returns to NIMBUS in the specification | 4.13.1, 4.13.8 |

(The plant table clause in 3.3 refers to "Section 5.4" for the export gate; 5.4 is the routing export's scheduling clause and the gate is 6.4. A slip in the Functional Specification, noted so nobody follows the wrong reference.)

**The finish-gate lead.** Section 6.4 says orders in the export are "fully gated by the plant's Planning Horizon ... plus 1 day ... This is relative to the `PLAF-PEDTR` end-date", then breaks off. If the limit is on the finish date, it conflicts with NIMBUS's own test for "absent from the snapshot", which keys on the start: an order is a deletion candidate when its SAP start is on or before the visibility end plus one day (`sap_staging.py:709-710`). Two orders then fall in the gap:

| Order | In SAP's export (limit on finish) | Deleted by NIMBUS as vanished (test on start) |
|---|---|---|
| Starts inside the horizon, finishes beyond horizon plus one day | No | Yes, on every apply |
| Finishes inside the horizon, started earlier | Yes (if no lower bound) | No |

The first row matters because NIMBUS's own Send can create it: a finish moved later (a push, a reversal, a long order whose finish crosses the edge) takes the order out of SAP's next export while NIMBUS still expects it. Example (illustrative): horizon edge Fri 6 Nov; order 1000234 starts Tue 3 Nov and the planner places its finish Mon 9 Nov and sends; SAP's next export omits it because its finish is now beyond Sat 7 Nov; NIMBUS archives it on the next apply (or holds the batch if enough orders do the same). The 25 percent hold would catch a bulk wave, not one or two orders. Whether the sentence ends the way it appears to, whether past finishes are excluded, and whether the limit is on start or finish are Appendix D items (D.1 item 7); the owner should confirm what the sentence was meant to say before anything is built on it.

This is relative to the PLAF –PEDTR end-date. The purpose of this is to gate the total size of the export to nimbus relative to.So, we will"`; `fsd2.txt:167`: "Presently unsure if Async or Sync RFC is better"; `fsd2.txt:370` (7.3): "Synchronous RFC would be the better fit – but timing/success of the ingestion is of high importance."; `fsd2.txt:139-140`, `:311-312`, `:382-383`: "The program will be scheduled via a Process Chain."
- `fsd2.txt:39-42` (3.3): "Frozen Horizon ... in days"; "Planning Horizon ... used to gate the planned order export (Section 5.4)".
- `docs/SAP_STAGING_DESIGN.md:161`: `"Staging-only: prvbe, paart, umskz, kdauf, rsnum, knttp, vfmng, gsbtr, kzavc, badi, dac_creation_date."`; `:54` (D22): "Trust that SAP's planning horizon and NIMBUS's visibility horizon are kept equal by hand".
- `sap_staging.py:709-710` and `743` as quoted in 4.13.1.
- `docs/SAP_STAGING_VALIDATION_PLAN.md` A5: "The SAP planning horizon and NIMBUS visibility horizon are kept equal per plant (D22) | Orders in the gap are deleted as "vanished" on every apply".

#### 4.13.7 The sample profile and the pilot feed are different things

**What the document's numbers rest on.** The headline figures in 1.2 and 8.11 come from the COOIS sample workbook (593 rows, sheet `Cleaned`, a stale extract dated 2026-08-17) and the Sequence_Testing workbook (328 rows). Both are manual Excel files. The document labels the first a production-order list; the repository does not record its object type, and the owner's record says the pilot intake is planned orders only (`aggregate_to_detail.md:664`: "the pilot is 100 % planned orders") **[unverified: the file's order category and order type columns would show which it is]**. Whichever it is, the numbers describe the manual Excel path on a routing-off plant. The SAP planned-order feed is a different path: it carries no run time, it is held while routing is off (`sap_staging.py:728-734`), and unlike the Excel file it carries an end time (FSD 6.5).

| Headline number | Rests on | Is it a property of the planned-order feed? | What settles it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 461 of 593 rows at or over the 168 h run-time bound | Machine Hours in the Excel file, a run time taken on routing-off plants only | No: the feed has no Machine Hours; its run time comes from the routing resolver | The resolver's output on the pilot plants (profile P3, 4.13.5) |
| Every finish is a bare date at midnight (593 of 593, 328 of 328) | The Excel files have no time-of-day column | Unknown: the feed carries an end time, but whether SAP fills it is not known | A first feed snapshot, or Appendix D, D.1 item 5 |
| 585 of 593 rows have a window shorter than the run time | Machine Hours, whose unit is unconfirmed (8.11 notes it looks like a sum across parallel machines) | Unknown for the feed's routing-derived run time | Profile P4 below |
| 26 of 593 rows have a finish equal to the start (and 328 of 328 in Sequence_Testing) | The Excel files | Unknown; a planned order normally has a distinct start and finish | A first feed snapshot |
| 9 of 507 rows would derive a start before 2026-10-13 | A stale extract; the document already says it understates reversals | Unknown | The live feed |
| The M1 midnight mechanism, the echo truth table, the guard sites | Code | Yes: they are code facts, independent of any sample | n/a |

**Which direction the first Send moves SAP's finish.** The document says an untouched order's first Send "already moves SAP's finish earlier" (2.1, 2.2, 4.5.1(a), 4.5.4). Today's Send transmits start plus run time in elapsed hours. If SAP's window is longer than that, the sent finish is earlier than SAP's (the document's examples: a 60 hour window against a 20 hour run time gives 40 hours earlier). If SAP's window is shorter, the sent finish is later than SAP's. For 585 of 593 sample rows the window is shorter than the Machine Hours, so for that sample the first Send would move SAP's finish later, not earlier. Which regime the pilot's planned orders are in is unknown until profiled. The benefit the rule claims (the first Send transmits the due date, identity) does not depend on the regime; only the sentence "moves earlier" does, and 2.1, 4.5.1(a) and 4.5.4 now carry the qualifier.

**The regime question for the new rule.** Under the new rule an untouched (never-placed) order sends nothing (OQ33 B1, 6.2) and a placed order sends its placed finish, so in neither regime does the first Send change SAP's finish for an untouched order; for a placed order it sends the finish the planner chose. What does depend on the regime is the derived start (4.13.3: a window shorter than the run time puts the start before SAP's start) and SAP's reaction to a finish moved by NIMBUS (4.13.2).

Profile P4, read-only, on orders that have both SAP dates (planned-order feed or Excel):

```sql
-- P4: does SAP's window cover the run time? (elapsed hours, as today's Send computes the finish)
SELECT plant, count(*) AS orders,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE run_time IS NULL)                                                       AS no_run_time,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE sap_basic_finish_date - sap_basic_start_date >= run_time * interval '1 hour') AS window_covers_run,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE sap_basic_finish_date - sap_basic_start_date <  run_time * interval '1 hour') AS window_shorter_than_run
  FROM orders
 WHERE sap_basic_start_date IS NOT NULL AND sap_basic_finish_date IS NOT NULL
 GROUP BY plant ORDER BY plant;
```

Evidence:
- `aggregate_to_detail.md:664`: "12. Which `ORDER_CATEGORY` / `ORDER_TYPE` values distinguish planned from production orders? — **Not known; the pilot is 100 % planned orders and roughly 90 % of all NIMBUS intake will be (repetitive manufacturing).**"
- `sap_staging.py:728-734`: `if not (info["routing_enabled"] and has_routing): held.append("routing_required")`; `docs/SAP_STAGING_DESIGN.md:55` (D23): "The planned-order export has no run time."
- Document 8.11 and 1.2 for the sample figures as reported; the second review did not re-derive them.
- `sap_staging.py:2210-2211`: `COALESCE(seg.first_start, scheduled_start, basic_start_date), COALESCE(seg.last_end, db._EFF_END_WITH_RUNTIME_MISMATCH_SQL)`; `db.py:212-217` (`_EFF_END_SQL`): start plus `run_time * INTERVAL '1 hour'`.

#### 4.13.8 SAP facts that must be settled before Send goes live

Send has no code gate. It needs an API key and the admin role (`backend/integration/routes.py:875`); the practical brake is the manual Mulesoft database role, the network access and the poll interval (`docs/DEPLOYMENT.md:35`: "Nothing flows until the role exists, Mulesoft has network access and the poll interval is set"). Section 7 and 8 own the release mechanism. This subsection owns the SAP facts.

**Assumption A9, promoted to a gate.** The validation plan's A9 ("send one order, read the next export, diff all fields", source SAP Development) has an owner and a pass bar but no place in the cutover sequence, and the only echo ever measured used a simulated SAP. It becomes a gate: **no admin presses Send on a production plant until A9 has a written answer from SAP Development.** The test is widened from one order to three, because the answers differ by order type:

| Test order | What to do | What to record, field by field |
|---|---|---|
| Unfirmed, finish moved later | Send a finish-only change; read the next export; wait for the next planning run and read the export after it | Finish date and time returned (exactly as sent? float added?); start (derived how?); quantity, version, firm flag unchanged?; did the order survive the run under the same number? |
| Firmed (flag X sent) | Send a finish-only change | Is the change accepted on a firmed order? Does SAP reschedule? Does the order survive the next planning run under the same number? |
| A finish that puts SAP's own derived start in the past | Send a finish earlier than SAP's lead time allows | Does SAP flip forward from today? What finish and start come back? To what rounding? |

Plus one reading on all three: is the time of day kept (send a finish with a non-zero time and read the end time back).

The other SAP facts the gate depends on:

| # | Fact | If wrong | How to settle | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Float on the imported finish, and basic against production dates (4.13.2) | The echo never matches; placement wiped | The A9 test | SAP Development |
| 2 | SAP's own reversal and tolerance (4.13.2) | A returned later finish overrides the held finish | The A9 test, third order | SAP Development |
| 3 | A finish-only change on a firmed order (4.13.1) | The firm flag NIMBUS sends gives no protection | The A9 test, second order | SAP Development |
| 4 | Does a firm flag set through the import stop the weekly planning run renumbering (4.13.1) | A frozen-window order drifts into firm and is still renumbered | Observe one order across a planning run | SAP Development |
| 5 | Time of day discarded or kept (4.5.5, case 3) | Echo widens to every evening finish | Read one export | SAP Development |
| 6 | SAP zone and Mulesoft pass-through (4.13.4) | Every converted time is off | One order with a known time | SAP Basis, integration owner |
| 7 | Cadence of the export and import process chains; sync or async (4.13.6) | The stale-snapshot window below has no known width | Ask for the chain schedule | SAP Development |
| 8 | Whether the import's skip-and-log reaches NIMBUS as a per-row error (4.13.1) | A Send for a deleted order reads `sent` | Mulesoft behaviour (assumption A8) | Integration owner |
| 9 | What the export's finish limit is (4.13.6) | Orders cycle in and out of the snapshot | Ask what the cut-off sentence says | Owner, SAP Development |
| 10 | What the commitment date means (4.6.3) | The late tile measures against the wrong date | The profile in 4.6.3, then ask | SAP Development |

**Profile P1, read-only: how much of the schedule is firmed.** It sizes the weekly renumbering effect in 4.13.1 and checks assumption A12 (whether the stored firm indicator is SAP's planned-order firm flag).

```sql
-- P1: firmed share per plant, and how many orders were archived as vanished in the last 30 days
SELECT plant, count(*) AS orders,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE upper(btrim(coalesce(firming_indicator, ''))) = 'X') AS sap_firmed,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE manual_firmed)                                       AS planner_firmed
  FROM orders GROUP BY plant ORDER BY plant;

SELECT plant, date_trunc('day', deleted_at) AS day, count(*) AS vanished_orders
  FROM sap_stage_vanished_order GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;   -- weekly waves show as spikes
```

**A first-class case: Send, send again, then a snapshot of the first send.** The code remembers only the latest sent finish per order (the next Send overwrites it; design D20, refined: "the sent values are not cleared by a planner edit; they are overwritten by the next Send"). So:

| Step | What happens | Stored by NIMBUS |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Planner places Order Z for finish F1, Send 1; SAP applies it | Remembered sent finish F1; baseline B (the last SAP-sent finish) |
| 2 | Planner revises to F2 and sends again before a snapshot reflecting F1 has arrived | Remembered sent finish F2 |
| 3 | A snapshot arrives that SAP exported after applying Send 1 and before applying Send 2: finish F1 | F1 differs from baseline B, and F1 is not F2: no echo, so "dates" is raised: the F2 placement and firm flag are wiped, the due date becomes F1, the baseline becomes F1 |
| 4 | The next snapshot carries F2 | F2 differs from baseline F1, but F2 equals the remembered sent finish: echo; nothing more happens |

Net result: SAP and NIMBUS both hold F2, but NIMBUS shows it as SAP's due date and the planner's placement and firm flag are gone. The window is the time between Send 2 and SAP applying it plus an export, whose width is unknown until the process-chain cadence is known (fact 7). A snapshot taken before SAP applies Send 1 at all carries the old finish B, equals the baseline, and does nothing. The case is already in the document as one clause ("a stale snapshot racing a second Send can misread an old echo", 4.5.3); it is repeated here because a planner who iterates (send, adjust, send) is exactly the person who triggers it. Options if the A9 test and the cadence show the window is real, none decided here: remember a short list of recently sent finishes per order instead of the last one; refuse a second Send of an order whose previous send has not yet been echoed; widen the echo test to any finish sent within a stated number of hours. Recommendation: put "send twice in quick succession" in the A9 test and decide once the cadence is known.

#### 4.13.9 Impact table for this section

| Surface | Today | Under the new rule | Severity | Anchors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Placement on an unfirmed order across the weekly planning run | Lost at the next run (at most a week at the pilot); archived 30 days | Same: the placed finish exists in NIMBUS but SAP replaces the order | high | `aggregate_to_detail.md:475`, `:665`; `sap_staging.py:709-710` |
| Echo rule against a renumbered order | Keyed on order id; cannot link old and new | Same | high | `db.py:123-126`, `3180` |
| Vanish hold under weekly renumbering | Trips only above 25 percent; below it, silent deletion | Recurring weekly; 8.9 examines the first apply only | high | `sap_staging.py:68`, `281-287` |
| The promise "the sent finish never moves" | Stated for every order | True of NIMBUS's holding; of SAP's holding only for firmed and frozen-window orders | high | 4.13.1 |
| What SAP does to a finish it is sent (float, reversal, rounding) | Unstated; echo measured on a simulator only | The same, now carrying the backward rule's finishes | high (gate: A9) | `docs/SAP_STAGING_VALIDATION_PLAN.md:42`, `:148` |

## 5. Reading B: just-in-time optimizer (separately decidable)

**This section can be accepted or deferred on its own as a decision. It is not self-contained as a design: it builds on a held, protected due date and on four other decisions, listed in 5.1a. Read 5.1a before accepting anything here.**

### 5.1 What it is, in business terms

Today the optimizer packs work to the left: every order lands as early as capacity allows, so finished goods sit in the warehouse until the due date. **Reading B** adds a just-in-time optimizer that places each order **as late as possible without missing its due date**, then walks backward through working hours, blackouts and setup. When the backward walk would start before the planning floor (normally now), it flips to forward from the floor (O2), accepts a late finish, and shows the lateness.

What B buys: less finished-goods inventory carried between finish and due date. Whether inventory is a NIMBUS goal is itself an owner question (OQ60): `PRODUCT.md:17` says success is on-time delivery, with utilization and changeover efficiency as a supporting concern, and does not mention inventory; `PRODUCT.md:33` makes due dates "the north star". B can trade slack for earliness; it cannot add on-time delivery. What it cannot buy: it cannot reduce lateness, and it leaves **zero slack**: an order placed to finish exactly at its due date turns late the moment anything grows.

Because B decides **when** an order finishes, it only has value if the finish is stored and sent to SAP (Reading A: every order stores a placed finish that is held, the start is derived backward from it, and the finish SAP was given never moves when a run time changes). B is therefore not independent of A on the server (5.8).

#### 5.1a Prerequisites and a recommendation, so section 5 can be read alone

| Prerequisite | Why Reading B needs it | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Blocker 1** (the first Send-and-echo overwrites the due date; guarded at the three write sites or the in-memory patch, OQ31) | B's ceiling, the latest finish an order may take, is computed from `original_end_date` (`frontend/optimization/engine.mts:1092`, `1114-1126`; `setup-scheduler.mts:1196-1199`, `6217-6229`). If a just-in-time finish is Sent and echoed back as the due date, the finish becomes its own target: lateness and the push ceiling are then measured against what NIMBUS chose, not what SAP asked for, and a plan that SAP would call late reads as on time | 4.5.3, OQ31 |
| **OQ23** (time of day of a date-only finish) | B needs a precise due instant; a date-only due read as midnight puts a just-in-time order on the previous evening | 4.5.5, OQ49 |
| **OQ13** (no contiguous slot ends at the held finish) | B's backward walk meets the same infeasible-finish case, and under the default `never` split policy an overlong order has no backward rule at all (the pilot sample is mostly overlong) | 4.2.3, OQ13 |
| **OQ14** (A-lite or A-strict) | the post-pass shares its backward placer with A-strict; under A-lite it is the first backward placer in the code | 4.8.11, 5.7 |

**Recommendation (mirrors OQ48; the decision is the owner's).** Only if OQ60 confirms that inventory is a goal, do the right-shift post-pass as an "align to due dates" option on the existing modes, after Phase 4 has shipped so that the held finish and the due-date guard are live; consider a full backward-search mode only if the owner wants sequence freedom for earliness; deferring B entirely is acceptable. Why: in the traced case 1 (5.2) the post-pass saves the same 106 hours of earliness as full B, for about 500 to 650 lines and 3 to 5 days against 2,100 to 3,000 lines and 3 to 5 weeks plus line parallelism for full B (inference, low confidence); and the product-fit question (OQ60) should be answered before either is built.

### 5.2 The three-case simulation (numbers corrected by cross-check)

Inputs (illustrative): one machine, Mon-Fri 06:00-18:00, no blackouts, no frozen horizon, split policy `never`. Orders: **A** 6 h due Wed 2026-10-21 18:00; **B** 4 h due Thu 10-22 12:00; **C** 8 h due Thu 10-22 18:00. Setup minutes: A to B 30, B to C 60, A to C 15; other transitions have no recorded setup (admitted at zero, counted as uncovered). The line's current state is A's. "Earliness" = due date minus placed finish, summed over orders.

| Case (sequence A, B, C) | Forward placement today | Just-in-time placement | Earliness forward / JIT | Late orders / lateness |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Now = Mon 08:00** | A Mon 08:00-14:00 (52 h early); B setup Tue 06:00-06:30, run 06:30-10:30 (**49.5 h early**); C setup Wed 06:00-07:00, run 07:00-15:00 (27 h early) | C setup Thu 09:00-10:00, run 10:00-18:00 (0 h early); B setup Wed 13:30-14:00, run 14:00-18:00 (18 h early); A Wed 07:30-13:30 (4.5 h early) | **128.5 h / 22.5 h** (saves 106 h) | 0 / 0 both; setup 90 min both |
| **2. Now = Thu 08:00 (everything already due)** | A Thu 08:00-14:00 (20 h late); B setup Fri 06:00-06:30, run 06:30-10:30 (22.5 h late); C setup Mon 10-26 06:00-07:00, run 07:00-15:00 (93 h late) | identical: a reversal domino keeps every order at its forward position | n/a | 3 late, 135.5 h, both |
| **3. Now = Wed 08:00 (partial)** | A Wed 08:00-14:00 on time; B Thu 06:30-10:30 on time; C Fri 07:00-15:00 (21 h late) | identical: A would start Wed 07:30 (before now), so A reverses to 08:00, B follows to Thu, C misses Thursday | n/a | 1 late, 21 h, both |

Reading the table: JIT only helps when there is slack (case 1). With a due-date-first sequence at Thu 08:00 (C, B, A: 2 late, 68 h, the fewest of the six sequences), a right-shift moves only C, from Thu 08:15-16:15 to Thu 10:00-18:00 (setup 09:45-10:00); lateness is unchanged. A two-hour slack buffer in case 1 changes only C (setup Thu 07:00-08:00, run 08:00-16:00); A and B are held by their successors. Correction recorded during the first edition's own cross-check: a claim that Due Date mode would choose a different sequence at Wed 08:00 is wrong; A, B, C is also the Due Date winner there (1 late, 21 h), so that example proves nothing about needing the search.

**Sequence sensitivity (case 1, JIT over all six sequences).** Earliness hours and uncovered transitions: A,B,C 22.5 h with 0 uncovered; A,C,B 48 h with 1; B,A,C 24 h with 1; B,C,A 114 h with 1; C,A,B 48 h with 1; C,B,A 72 h with 2. The earliness-best sequence is the one the forward search already picks (the only fully covered one), so the extra sequence freedom of a full backward search buys nothing in this case. Whether it matters on real plants depends on cases where sequences are close in lateness and coverage `[unverified: one small case only]`.

No prototype exists and no benchmark was run.** Existing tests need no reclassification only if B is an **added** mode; if B replaces a forward mode, the forward-pinned tests (about 187 in the setup-scheduler file, about 108 in the engine file) need rewriting or dual running.

### 5.4 Shape: forward admission, backward placement

Placing the successor first makes its setup depend on a predecessor that might still be dropped. Example: sequence A, X, C; C is placed with setup from X; if X then fails to place, C's setup should have been from A and C is already placed. The clean answer: decide **admission first** with a forward pass (which the existing evaluator already does) and run the backward pass over the admitted subsequence only. The alternative (treat a mid-sequence failure as an infeasible candidate) loses today's never-freeze behaviour for that candidate. The same shape makes the right-shift post-pass correct by construction. Because the search evaluates whole sequences, each order's predecessor is known when it is placed; a constructive backward dispatch that picks "the next order" backward could not know it, and the existing architecture avoids that case.

### 5.5 Reversal boundary, setup, frozen, tails

- **Reversal boundary is the planning floor, not literally now:** the later of the planning start and now, then per-order frozen-end and pull floors (`engine.mts:2046-2048`, `2184`). A planner picking a planning start a week out gets a reversal point a week out; a plant with a 2-day frozen horizon gets late orders starting no earlier than the end of the frozen window.
- **Reversal domino.** One reversed order pushes every later order forward until slack absorbs it (case 3 above turned an on-time chain into a late one).
- **Setup before the start.** Validation requires setup in the same contiguous operating time right before the production start (`6577-6584`). A backward placement must keep them together; allowing setup across a closed gap (one reading of OQ2) needs a validation change, the Gantt setup bars and the observation derivation. Fragments stay decoupled in setup terms because the protected orders between them have known states.
- **Frozen decided by start.** A JIT order is never placed into the frozen window by a run (placements are floored at the frozen end), but the frozen band reaches each JIT order as days pass and then it is immovable; whether frozen is judged on start or derived finish is OQ4.
- **Unknown-setup tail** is placed at the late end of the fragment, not each at its own due date: a visible deviation from pure JIT for plants with many blank signatures.
- **Gap fill, Remove Backlog, auto-reflow** stay forward for a first cut.
- **Siblings:** a just-in-time pass tends to align the finishes of distribution children, spreading their starts and raising separation warnings (warnings only), **but only where each line has room**: a pass moves an order no later than its ceiling, and a protected order after it (firmed, running or frozen, `setup-scheduler.mts:6382`) is a hard ceiling for the order before it. Example (illustrative): two children on different lines with the same due Fri 16:00; line 1 has a firmed order starting Fri 14:00 right after the child, so that child's latest finish is Fri 14:00 and the pair finishes two hours apart. Read "aligns" as "aligns where capacity allows". The separation finding (`setup-scheduler.mts:6720-6730`) will still fire for the rest.

**The due instant on a closed day, and the optimizer functions that change (OQ49).** OQ49's lead option reads the due instant "per OQ23" (the end of that date's working window). That is undefined for a due date on a closed day: a date-only due Sat 24 Oct on a Mon-Fri plant has no working window that date. The answer needs a named calendar (the line's, the plant's, or the default) and a rule (the previous open window's close, the next open window's close, or the calendar day's end), and it interacts with the push ceiling, which is midnight of the due date plus N plus 1 days (a Saturday due with N = 1 puts the ceiling at Mon 00:00, which no open window ends on). Example (illustrative): due Sat 24 Oct 00:00, push limit 1 day; "previous open window" gives Fri 22:00 as the due instant while the ceiling is Mon 00:00, so a just-in-time order may land up to a weekend plus Monday's hours after its own due instant and still be inside the cap. Today four places read the raw midnight and would each change or be changed by this choice: `dueTimestamp` (`setup-scheduler.mts:1196-1199`), `allowedPlanningWindow` (`6217-6229`), `Engine.earliestAllowedStart` and `Engine.latestAllowedEnd` (`engine.mts:1084-1126`), and the two lateness tallies (`setup-scheduler.mts:3002-3008`, `7186-7199`). They should share one helper (4.10.4 lists the same sites from the lateness side).

### 5.6 Worker, budget and scale

**Worker.** The post-pass, and a one-mode serial full B, need one new mode literal and optional request fields (slack, missing-due policy); due dates already travel inside the task snapshot, and validation is direction-neutral, so the serialized validation descriptor does not change. That holds for a **single serial search**. Full B with the line parallelism that the budget below calls practically required is not a mode literal: the optimizer plan calls it "an evaluator refactor plus a two-hop Worker protocol, not 'split the lines and merge the patches'" (`Optimizer_Update_10_06.MD:584`), because the keep-the-new-plan-or-revert judgement covers the whole plant at once (`finalizeCandidate`); its effort is corrected to 5 to 7 days (`:502`) and three owner questions are open there (`:677-679`): whether planners want the same answer as today or a better per-line one (blocks the parallel version), which lines are optimized when time runs out (informs it), and what hardware planners run (blocks the core cap). Two of the three block line parallelism; this document does not decide them. Also see 4.8.8: any new request or response field needs a version or tolerance rule for old tabs.

**Budget (controls carry over unchanged):** 5,000 ms shared deadline (`engine.mts:562`); 20,000 iterations per line times lines in scope (`557`, `2168`); exact search only up to 500 orderings **and** at most 8 state groups (`setup-scheduler.mts:1984`, `engine.mts:556`); convergence stop after 2,000 non-improving candidates (`setup-scheduler.mts:804`); neighbourhood 16 insertion plus 16 swap moves. Per candidate a backward pass costs about the same as forward (with a reverse scan and early stop); a candidate that hits the floor also needs the forward pass, so the cost is about 1x with no reversal and up to about 2x on a backlog-heavy plant. **Both of those factors are estimates from reading the code; nothing was measured.**

**What the optimizer plan actually measured, as three different quantities.** On the 70-line, 30-orders-per-line shape: (1) after its first speed-ups, Min Changeover hit the 5 s deadline at **7.2 s wall with 55 of 70 lines searched and 15 left untouched** (`Optimizer_Update_10_06.MD:476`); (2) a later run found every line searched in every mode, with wall times of **2.2 to 4.9 s** for Min Changeover, 1.8 to 4.2 s for SPT and 2.8 to 4.3 s for Due Date, and drew the conclusion that "the 5 s deadline sits inside that noise, so on a slower laptop the same plant gets a different answer" (`:498`); (3) after the speed trims now in the code (T1 and T3), the median wall for the same shape fell from 2.09 s to **1.16 s** for Min Changeover (`:700`). The wall figures are benchmark times that include a separate one-second gap-fill pass after the search (`scripts/bench-optimizer.mjs:343-349`); the 5 s deadline bounds the search only (`engine.mts:562`, `2176`). So "2.2 to 4.9 s against a 5 s deadline" (the first edition's wording of this section) compared wall time with a deadline, and was measured before the trims. With the trims, a 1x to 2x factor on a median of about 1.2 s leaves headroom on the machine measured and not necessarily on a slower one; the earlier conclusion that a 1-2x factor "pushes it past the deadline on most machines" is therefore not established either way, and 4.8.13 explains why a deadline-bound answer matters under A. All three measurements are quoted, not re-measured **[unverified: measured on the optimizer plan author's machine]**.

**Why the cost figures are not evidence.** The benchmark gives every order a due date within about plus or minus half a horizon of a base instant (`bench-optimizer.mjs:86`) and an identical floor and ceiling (`notBefore: () => now`, `notAfter: () => horizonEnd`, `254-255`), so it has no pull or push limit, no missing, past or beyond-horizon due dates, and its single plant row (`217-224`) has no frozen horizon, no firmed orders and no split-order policy. It therefore cannot exercise B's expensive cases. A fixture for B should add: a share of orders with no due date, due dates before now and beyond the horizon; plant pull and push limits of the pilot's values; firmed, running and frozen orders; `never` and `overlong_only` split policies with overlong orders; and distribution siblings. The post-pass's "well under 5 percent" is likewise an estimate, not a result. At the 70-line target scale, line parallelism (the deferred 5-7 day item) is practically required for full B **if** the larger factor is real; the neighbour generator concentrates changes at the front of a sequence, which matters least backward, so it must vary the tail (about 30 lines, easy to forget); and a due date beyond the horizon end reintroduces uncapped per-call day walks unless the ceiling is clamped to the horizon (default horizon is 35 days from planning start).

### 5.7 The right-shift post-pass alternative

After the normal forward search and gap fill, walk each line from the last order to the first and move every movable order as late as it can go without passing its due date (or push cap), **without reordering, without changing setup minutes, never earlier than its forward position**. Orders already late, protected, running, or whose ceiling is below their forward end do not move, so the reversal falls out for free. Late count, lateness minutes, setup, uncovered edges, priority order and sequence are unchanged by construction (it cannot worsen the eight-wide score; it does raise instability, and the preview does not show that: see below). In the case 1 trace the post-pass result is identical to full backward.

**What the preview shows when only finishes move.** The post-pass runs on every scheduled order, so the start of every shifted order changes. Instability is the minutes between old and new start (`setup-scheduler.mts:2999-3000`, `7202-7203`) and rises, but the Optimize preview's verdict scores only three targets, changeovers, late count and late hours (`optimize-ui.mts:1633-1642`); the other cards are context. A post-pass plan that rewrites many finishes later therefore reads "neutral" ("no change") while the planner is about to Send SAP a set of changed finishes. The preview also carries no count of orders whose finish changes, only lines changed or unchanged (`optimize-ui.mts:1701`, `1777`). The decision the owner needs is whether Reading B's preview must show "N finishes move, the latest by H hours" next to the verdict, and whether a shift of orders the planner did not expect to move should be blocked, confirmed, or allowed. Example (illustrative): a plant of 300 orders; the post-pass moves 140 finishes later by an average of 30 hours; changeovers, late count and late hours are unchanged, so the verdict is neutral, and 140 changed finishes go to SAP at the next Send. Severity: medium.

Size: 500-650 source lines, 300-450 test lines, 3-5 days (inference); reuses the winner, the interval index, the setup lookup, validation and metric refresh, and hooks in after gap fill (`engine.mts:884-889`). It cannot reuse auto-reflow (main thread, forward only) or the existing placer with a clip (it returns the earliest fit, not the latest, and time-reflecting the intervals puts production before setup).

**What it cannot do versus full B:** choose sequences for earliness; reduce lateness (late orders stay put); re-pack the freed early capacity (leftovers placed by gap fill stay early); add admission freedom (the admitted set is whatever forward admitted). It still needs a backward placer (shared with Reading A strict, the option of re-deriving the start of every optimizer result from its finish, 4.8.11), and the shifted finish becomes the placed finish sent to SAP.

### 5.8 B is not independent of A on the server

"Reading B alone needs no server change" holds only under today's effective-end expression and only until the next run-time change. A JIT result has zero slack, so the drift of the A/B/C simulation (4.8.6: after order B's run time grows from 4 h to 6 h, the server shows its finish 2 h later and the browser's repair shows it 18 h later) becomes lateness immediately. B inherits every server and re-derivation blocker of Reading A.

### 5.10 Reading B's own decisions (not decided here)

Each row is a separate point that its owner question has to settle. Rows are grouped by question, so a question that carries several points repeats its id in the first column: OQ48 four points, OQ49 three, OQ9 two. Every row is a point inside the named question, not a further question.

| OQ48 | Mode versus option | a fourth mode (the alternate-plan table then runs it too) or an "align to due dates" checkbox on any mode (the post-pass). Folding JIT into Min Changeover contradicts the settled promise that due date is not an objective there |
| OQ48 | Unknown-setup tail at the late end | accept the deviation from pure JIT |
| OQ48 | Accept or defer B as a phase | the post-pass is the cheap first cut (3-5 days); full B is 3-5 weeks plus line parallelism at scale |
| OQ48 | Prerequisites | blocker 1, OQ2, OQ13, OQ14, OQ23 and Phase 2's server contract (5.1a); Reading B is not accepted in isolation |
| OQ49 | Due-date instant versus day end | the push cap uses due midnight plus N + 1 days; a due date at 00:00 reads as the previous evening; JIT needs a precise instant |
| OQ49 | Missing or beyond-horizon due date | place forward ASAP, leave queued, or clamp to the horizon end (puts the order at the very end of the window, far from its due date); a due date at or before the floor is a reversal |
| OQ49 | Due instant on a closed day, and which functions change | undefined for a due date on a closed day: which calendar and which rule, and how it meets the push ceiling (5.5, last paragraph); four read points change together (`dueTimestamp`, `allowedPlanningWindow`, the `Engine` floor and ceiling, the two lateness tallies) |
| OQ9 | Slack buffer | zero by default; a 2 h buffer in case 1 moves only C; what buffer protects against run-time drift |
| OQ9 | Tardiness, priority, changeover ranking | earliness as a side fact beside the pinned 8-wide score; after lateness and before priority (due-date-driven JIT), after setup (rarely changes anything), or a weighted sum (separate, larger change) |
| OQ4 | Frozen judged on start or derived finish | JIT rolls into the frozen band over time |
| OQ11 | Distribution siblings | accept aligned finishes, spread starts, more separation warnings |
| OQ60 | Product fit | whether finished-goods inventory is a NIMBUS goal at all (`PRODUCT.md:17`, `33`); B's benefit is less inventory, not more on-time delivery |

## 6. Data and schema

### 6.1 Fields by role

See the table in 3.2. In short: the due date lives in `orders.basic_finish_date` (wire `original_end_date`) provided three alterations are closed (hygiene fabrication, client rewrite, echo overwrite); the placed finish is `orders.scheduled_end` or a new column (6.2); the derived start is `orders.scheduled_start` plus, for split orders, the first segment start; the change-detection baselines are the two as-sent columns. For a row with a placed finish the server-computed pieces (V1 to V4) lose arm 1 (start plus run time) in the read formula in either option. For a row never placed, arm 1 survives or goes as the read rule of 6.2 decides (pending OQ33).

### 6.2 Options raised: re-purpose `scheduled_end` or add a column

Not decided here (OQ32; the cutover rule for existing rows is OQ5 and OQ33). The facts and the consequences, per option:

| Aspect | Re-purpose `scheduled_end` | New placed-finish column |
|---|---|---|
| Read formula | drop arm 1; becomes stored end then due date; V2 collapses into it | placed finish, with the legacy arms as fallback while unmigrated, later stored end then due date; a NULL means "never finish-anchored" and falls back lazily |
| Existing rows | every non-NULL stored end becomes authority at deploy; an identity-preserving cutover needs a backfill writing today's effective end for every planner-touched row; that backfill is an UPDATE and bumps xmin on each, so every open editor goes stale | no mass write is forced: a NULL keeps the legacy result (start plus run time) until a save or an optimizer Apply writes the column. That also means a placed row's end still moves with a run-time change until the column is written, so the identity write of 8.2 (placed rows only) is what makes the held finish hold for existing orders at the first run-time change after release; 8.13 step 3 therefore still runs one UPDATE, against the new column. Never-placed rows are the lazy NULL (read rule below) |
| DTOs | unchanged (`end_date` already writes this column) | unchanged if the wire keeps `end_date`; the write target in `_order_update_shape` (`db.py:1107-1112`) changes |
| xmin | unchanged mechanism; the backfill is the only event | unchanged mechanism |
| Reset, queue and hold writers | already null the stored end | must also null the new column at `db.py:1106`, `3665`, `sap_staging.py:1799`, `resolver.py:769` and the resolver tests; a missed site leaves a ghost anchor |
| Constraints and flags | `chk_orders_sched_range` and the user-scheduled flag already cover it | needs its own check and an addition to `USER_SCHEDULED` (`db.py:559`); `chk_orders_sched_range` would not cover it |
| Other end-formula copies | purge and diagnostics already prefer the stored end; remove arm 1 in `db.py:212-217`, `setup/data.py:498-511`, `db.py:3221-3225` | same copies plus add the column to purge, the slot echo (`db.py:2641-2642`), the chunk read (`db.py:3160-3166`), outbound, setup, the running test |
| Rollback after planner edits | old code ignores the promoted value when run time is set and shows start plus run time; nothing corrupt | same visible outcome; legacy values pristine |
| Migration discipline | data-mutating; the deploy runner's destructive-keyword gate (`ALTER`, `DROP`, `DELETE`, `UPDATE`, `TRUNCATE`, `RENAME`, `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, comments included; `.claude/skills/promote-azure/scripts/apply-migrations.ps1:67`, `74-76`) releases every pending matching file at once | additive; lazy conversion needs no data-mutating step |

Evidence leans to a new column if the cutover must be lazy, identity-preserving and rollback-friendly, because historical stored ends are an unmarked mixture (start plus run time at save time, stale after run-time changes, flat SAP-window widths, edge-resize leftovers; WS07-13 INFERENCE, medium confidence) that cannot be separated without a full backfill. Re-purposing touches fewer files but forces that backfill and a coordinated xmin bump. The save path today stores whatever width the client sends, and the browser always sends both edges, so for browser-placed orders the stored end equals start plus run time at the moment of the save (WS01-3, FACT for the sent values; the client computing it that way is WS04).

Conflict between OQ5's identity-preserving cutover and O4 for **never-placed** orders (WS07 simulation 4): Order Z unplaced shows Mon 06:00 to Tue 02:00 today. O4's default (placed finish defaults to the due date) puts the bar at Tue 14:00 to Wed 18:00, 32 h later at the start and 40 h later at the end. Identity would instead seed the placed finish with today's effective end (Tue 02:00), which is not the due date. For never-placed rows the two cannot both hold: seed once per row, or keep a lazy NULL fallback until first touch. Owner decision; SQL can make identity only for rows with a stored start that are not queued, split or flag-held (ADJ-WS15 R1, R2); the Gantt for never-placed rows shows a calendar-dependent client snap (`persistence.mts:953`, `975-977`), so identity for them must be a read-time fallback.

#### The read rule for a row that has never been placed (stated once; every other section points here)

**Pending OQ33: option B, start plus run time computed at read time, is the recommendation; the document's examples assume B for any row nobody has placed unless an example says it assumes option A.** A never-placed row is an order with no stored start, no stored end, no segments, not queued (8.2). Placed rows are unaffected: the stored placed finish wins for them in every option. For a never-placed row the rule has these parts.

| Question | Recommended option B | Option A | Option C |
|---|---|---|---|
| What the board and every server reader show | Today's served bar: SAP start plus run time in elapsed hours. The "derived start" of such a row is SAP's start; no backward walk is run | Placed finish seeded from the due date; start derived backward | The browser's forward snap on top of the served value (history-dependent) |
| What Send does | **B1 (recommended): the row is not an outbound candidate until it has a placed finish.** B2 (a variant the owner can choose inside B): it sends today's served value | Sends the due date | Unchanged: sends the served value (a snapped bar and the sent value can still differ) |
| Is the due date the fallback for the bar? | No | Yes | No |
| Lateness | As today for unsnapped rows; for the snapped class the bar moves by the snap delta, so lateness moves with it | End equals the due date by construction, so lateness reads 0 for every such row | As today |
| Moves a bar at cutover? | Not for unsnapped rows; the snapped class shifts to the unsnapped served value (8.3) | Every such bar | No |

Where the document says "the due date is the fallback only for orders never placed" (4.1.2, 7.4 item 1) or that "Send transmits the same value as today for every never-placed row" (8.3 option B, risk R1) it describes option A or B2, not the recommendation. Those places are conformed to this rule.

### 6.3 The due-date store question

| Option | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Keep it in `basic_finish_date` with an echo guard at the three write sites (4.5.3) | smallest schema change; depends on the sent-memory row existing (cascades away on purge, not restored on archive restore) and on SAP not moving the finish to a calendar boundary |
| A new immutable "due date as received" column written once and advanced only on a genuine SAP change | survives purge/restore ordering and the echo by construction; needs a new column on orders, the header and children, and a backfill from `sap_basic_finish_date` where non-NULL |
| `sap_basic_finish_date` as the store | rejected by the evidence: it follows every echo, is NULL when SAP sent none, is not on the wire (WS07-7) |

Either survivor must cover the header table and children (GAP03-6, GAP03-7). Production-version validity (4.5.12) is a separate anchor decision that interacts with this one.

### 6.4 `sap_basic_finish_date`: population and history

The column was added by `migrations/2026-10-06-sap-truth-firming.sql:8` (commit `9e1ce21`, 2026-10-06), so it is NULL for any row written before that; Azure apply was recorded in memory on 2026-10-08 [unverified on the live database]. It is written only by ingest (`db.py:2836`; values from `4045` and `4204`; fallback `3535`; the distribution child path `1376`, `1510`). It is NULL when the file had no finish (`db.py:3961`), and after the first Send plus echo it is overwritten with the placed finish (`db.py:2828-2829`, `2835-2836`, `2764-2765`). Restore source validity therefore ends at the first echo: **snapshot it before the first Send and before cutover**. A third ingest feeder of the fallback at `db.py:3535` is the inert pull-sync skeleton (`backend/integration/sap_sync.py:774`). The vanish archive copies the whole row opaquely (`db.py:2000`, `2074-2079`), and the admin table browser exposes both finish columns raw.

### 6.5 Backfill considerations (if a backfill is chosen)

From ADJ-WS15 R2, R3, R10, R11 and ADJ-WS01 Q01.6: exclude queued rows (`orders_planning_state_check` forbids stored dates there, `schema.sql:1969-1976`); exclude 2 or more segments (envelope rules, `db.py:1533-1537`, `1543-1549`); exclude mismatch-flagged rows (`db.py:258-263`); exclude rows with no stored start; exclude run time NULL with a stored end; exclude run time 0 where the target is not after the stored start (`chk_orders_sched_range`); exclude run time at or over 168 h (E9: an unvalidated violating row would fail any UPDATE of itself, `schema.sql:117-121`); skip rows already identical. Write and compare at second precision (the wire is seconds, `routes.py:194`, `db.py:861`) to avoid unseen fractional-second writes and needless xmin bumps. A restricted write set leaves the user-scheduled flag unchanged; the residual old-code readers of a rewritten stored end are the purge selector (`db.py:1829`), the slot echo (`db.py:2641-2642`) and diagnostics (`db.py:2189`); an unrestricted write (never-placed rows) flips the flag and stops the browser snap for those rows. The ordering of the first apply of SAP staging against the cutover is analysed in section 8 (staging code ships dormant, `brain.py:430`; cutover-first lets the first apply's reset wipe placed finishes wherever SAP's dates differ).

### 6.6 The `chk_orders_sched_range` fact

`chk_orders_sched_range` (`schema.sql:94-97`) is declared `NOT VALID` and exists only in `schema.sql`, not in any dated migration. Azure very likely has it NOT VALID via the 2026-06-30 `-f schema.sql` bootstrap (`docs/DEPLOYMENT.md:135-137`; INFERENCE). Consequences: it is enforced on every new write and re-checked on every UPDATE of an existing row, so pre-existing inverted rows would make any update of that row fail; a new placed-finish column would not be covered by it and would need its own check. The 168 h run-time bound (`chk_orders_run_time_bounds`, `schema.sql:117-121`) is a representation limit independent of anchor.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| New column vs re-purpose | n/a | owner decision | high | 6.2 table | none |
| Due-date store | mixed, overwritten | single protected store | blocker | `db.py:2829`, `distribution/data.py:1174`, `1355` | none pin the overwrite |
| `sap_basic_finish_date` | NULL pre-2026-10-06; follows echo | snapshot before first Send | medium | `db.py:2836`, `3961` | `tests/test_ingest_data_layer.py:1000-1009` |
| Backfill | none | exclusion list E1 to E9 (E9, run time at or over 168 h, belongs in the predicate and in gate G-6); xmin storm | high | `schema.sql:1969-1976`, `db.py:1533-1549` | none |
| `chk_orders_sched_range` | NOT VALID, schema.sql only | consider validation and a twin for any new column | low | `schema.sql:94-97` | none |
